fact: UNESCO recognizes the right to access information held by public bodies as a basic human right supporting democracy and government transparency.
A trustworthy information source is one that uses verification methods, discloses potential bias fairly, and stays open to correction when it errs.
As of January 2021, roughly 60% of the world's population, about 4.66 billion people, were using the Internet.
Journalism's core discipline of verification means checking facts, staying transparent about methods, and relying on original reporting rather than mere assertion.
News selection is often judged by timeliness and impact, but content can also be chosen for its drama or entertainment value instead of real importance.
Social media and search platforms are usually treated as neutral platforms rather than publishers, so they often face no legal liability for false content that spreads there.
Republishing content without credit can mislead audiences about its origin, which is one reason attributing original reporting and sources matters when sharing.
To judge whether a publication is trustworthy, check the author's expertise, the publisher's editorial process, and whether it went through peer review.
Primary sources present original first-hand data, secondary sources summarize or cite primary material, and tertiary sources compile many sources together, like an encyclopedia.
Search engines like Google automatically insert 'AND' between search terms, so results may only contain your words scattered separately, not together as a phrase.
Original creative work is automatically protected by copyright the moment it's created, so reusing someone else's content without permission can infringe even if never registered.
A 2018 MIT study of Twitter found that false stories spread farther, faster, and more broadly than true ones across every category of information.
UNESCO avoids the term 'fake news' since content that's fake isn't news at all; 'false' or 'misleading content' are more precise and harder to weaponize.
False and misleading content falls into distinct types, including impostor content, fabricated content, and manipulated content, each using a different deceptive technique.
Hateful and false content are often distinct, but expressions of hate are frequently supercharged with misleading claims to make them more convincing.
Conspiracy theories are often dressed up to look like investigative journalism, which is part of what makes them convincing.
Before sharing something online, it helps to ask whether you were aware it could be false, and what motivated you to spread it anyway.
Algorithms can amplify and actively recommend hateful or false content and the groups producing it, raising questions about whether platforms owe users a warning.
Advertisers can identify and track users through their digital footprints, targeting them with tailored content without the person ever asking for it or knowing it's tailored.
Media messages are never neutral; every text carries a bias that supports or challenges existing hierarchies of power, privilege, and pleasure.
Every piece of content has a purpose, often commercial or governmental, shaped by whoever created it, so it pays to ask why a text was made.
A 2015 global study found women made up just 24% of the people heard, read about, or seen in newspaper, TV, and radio news.
A 2018 global survey found 64% of women journalists had faced online abuse, including threats; most never reported it, and 38% self-censored afterward.
News images can obliterate information that wasn't captured on camera; what a photo leaves out shapes public memory as much as what it includes.
Social media platforms aren't passive spaces users simply act on; they're systems built on algorithms that actively determine which content succeeds.
Creators who gain the most followers or likes on a platform become the algorithm's favored voices, its most amplified opinion-leaders and tastemakers.
Tailored ads and recommendations are shaped by a person's own data trail, which can quietly narrow what they see rather than broadening it.
Photos shared online can carry hidden time and location metadata, potentially revealing exactly where and when a picture was taken.
Over 132 countries have adopted data protection laws based on international standards, though privacy protections still vary widely between them.
Once information is posted online, it becomes hard to control and can exist far longer than intended, visible to people the poster never met.
Before sharing photos or comments about someone else, it's worth asking who you're sharing with and whether that person would want it shared at all.
Different search engines can return different results about the same person; comparing results across engines reveals how differently each one profiles you.
Grooming attacks build on a child's longing for friendship, using platforms built for personal contact; mobile phones increase vulnerability since children are often unsupervised.
Merging profile data across platforms lets companies build a fuller picture of a person than any single platform holds, sometimes sold to data brokers.
User-generated content isn't checked by an independent source, so it can be partial, biased, or simply inaccurate if treated uncritically.
Algorithms can recommend groups or content built around harmful ideas, like idealized body types, specifically to keep users engaged for longer.
Content that provokes shock or offense isn't automatically 'harmful' under international human-rights standards; real harm requires more than causing discomfort.
So-called 'dog whistles' look like ordinary, legitimate content on the surface but function as a coded call to harmful action for those who recognize it.
Sharing fact-checking resources and calling out misinformation when you see it helps establish you as a trusted source others can rely on.
A political consultant advised clients that persuasion is '80% emotion and only 20% intellect,' a reminder that political ads are built to make you feel, not think.
Targeted ads let a campaign send different, even contradictory messages to different individuals based on how likely each one is to respond.
Undisclosed sponsorships behind influencer endorsements and paid product placement count as hidden advertising, since audiences aren't told the content was paid for.
AI is never neutral; it's built by humans with particular perspectives, and its algorithms and data sets are always skewed in some way.
Most virtual assistants are given a specific gender by their designers, and their programmed answers reflect particular worldviews and biases.
Deepfakes can often be spotted by checking for physically implausible details: mismatched skin texture, shadows that don't match the lighting, or unnatural blinking.
In a classic experiment, people shown slides of a car accident easily absorbed inaccurate details fed to them afterward and misremembered what happened.
A 'filter bubble' is algorithmic, filtering out content that doesn't match your past behavior; an 'echo chamber' is social, where contradicting information gets discounted by your community.
Some research finds people are actually exposed to more diverse content online than the 'filter bubble' theory predicts, challenging the popular narrative.
Fake accounts and bots are widely used in social media manipulation strategies, attacking opposition groups, spreading distracting messages, or coordinating harassment.
As of 2014, an estimated 245 million surveillance cameras were in use worldwide, so many that AI does most of the watching and flagging, not humans.
AI's 'black box' problem, where a system can't explain its own decision, makes it hard to know why an automated system flagged or rejected something.
A 2015 survey found roughly a third of Black, Hispanic, and white respondents felt minority groups are portrayed poorly in video games.
In some video games, women are shown sexualized and skimpily dressed while men are portrayed as strong and violent, reinforcing gender stereotypes for young players.
Digital games often collect player data; it's worth asking whether it's used only to improve the game or sold on for micro-targeted advertising.
Monopolistic ownership of media can threaten diversity and pluralism just as much as state control does, by concentrating who decides what the public sees.
A useful check on media bias: separately-owned outlets normally criticize each other's reporting, while outlets under one owner can end up just promoting themselves.
Journalists are generally expected to verify facts and disclose their methods, while protecting the confidentiality of sources who would otherwise face retaliation for speaking up.
